title: Colorado OAC Workers' Compensation Decision — WC 5-309-389-003
text:
Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 5-309-389-003
Issues
Whether Claimant proved by a preponderance of the evidence that he sustained
⮚
a compensable injury arising out of the course of his employment with Employer
on April 11, 2025.
Whether Claimant established by a preponderance of the evidence entitlement to
⮚
reasonable and necessary medical benefits to cure or relieve the effects of an
industrial injury.
If compensable, determination of Claimant’s authorized treating physician (ATP).
⮚
If compensable, whether Claimant established by a preponderance of the
⮚
evidence entitlement to temporary disability benefits.
If compensable, determination of Claimant’s average weekly wage (AWW).
⮚
Whether Claimant established that Respondent is subject to penalties for failure
⮚
to carry workers’ compensation insurance.
Findings of Fact
1. Claimant testified that on April 11, 2025, he was working for Employer removing
window trim when he heard a “snap” in his elbow. At approximately 9:00 a.m.,
Claimant sent a text message to Employer’s owner, Scott DeThomas indicating
that he had just injured his right shoulder and heard something snap while
removing window trim.
2. One of Claimant’s coworkers took him to the emergency department at UC
Health on April 11, 2025, where he was evaluated for acute shoulder pain that
occurred while he was removing siding. On examination, Claimant was noted to
have limited internal rotation of the right shoulder, with generalized tenderness.
The ER physician noted that Claimant’s presentation was most consistent with a
1

labrum tear or ligamentous injury, medical records also indicate Claimant may
have sustained a sprain. Claimant was discharged in a shoulder sling, with
instructions to rest and ice his shoulder, provided exercises for shoulder rotation,
and instructed to follow up with his primary care provider.
3. Between April 14, 2025 and April 18, 2025, Claimant and Mr. DeThomas
engaged in multiple text exchanges. On April 14, 2025, Claimant sent Mr.
DeThomas photos of the discharge instructions he received from UC Health. Mr.
DeThomas requested copies of work restrictions and indicated that his
“insurance does not cover unsubstantiated claims.” Claimant sent Mr. DeThomas
a note from UCHealth indicating that he may return to work on April 15, 2025.
4. In an April 15, 2025 text exchange, Claimant texted Mr. DeThomas: “I’ve never
been given any information on what doctors I can be seen by under workmen’s
comp.” To which Mr. DeThomas replied “…you haven’t asked and haven’t
provided any reason. Based on Fridays visit this wouldn’t have been a wc claim.
It said there might be a slight sprain and you’d be back to work today;” and
indicated “We can definitely make a claim if you believe it’s warranted. I’ve been
given no reason up to today when I asked you.”
5. Claimant then indicated that he needed a couple of days to recover and hopefully
return to working condition. Mr. DeThomas stated that “without a note or
diagnosis,” he could not pay Claimant and “a WC claim can’t proceed.” Mr.
DeThomas then requested that Claimant work at the office the following day
answering phones.
6. On April 17, 2025, Claimant was seen by Craig Lewis at County Line
Chiropractic, where he reported pain in his trapezius, right shoulder and arm,
chest and neck. It was noted that Claimant had limited right shoulder movement,
with difficulty hinging at the AC joint, and lifting from his deltoid. The treatment
Claimant received appears to have been directed to other body parts, including
his thoracic spine, lumbar spine, cervical spine, and hips.
7. On April 18, 2025, Claimant and Mr. DeThomas engaged in another text
exchange, Claimant again requested a list of physicians to see for a workers’
2

compensation claim. Claimant indicated he had contacted his primary care
provider and was informed that he did not treat worker’s compensation injuries.
Mr. DeThomas told Claimant to see his primary care physician as directed by the
ER physician, indicated that Claimant’s physician should speak to Employer’s
insurance agent, and sent Claimant the contact information for ,
who is apparently Employer’s insurance agent.
8. Claimant returned to County Line Chiropractic on April 30, 2025 with the same
complaints. Neither of the chiropractic records appear to document treatment
related to a ligamentous or labral injury to the right shoulder, with the exception
of applying a hot pack.
9. Respondent submitted a statement from in which
indicated that “A claim was not filed due to this being a nonwork-related injury
and was due to pre-existing condition or tissue degradation over time. Refusal to
return to work and was out of state on two separate occasions.” The remainder of
statement is a “timeline of events” which purports to set forth the
facts of what occurred regarding Claimant’s injury and claim. The vast majority of
statement appears to be information gathered from others, for
which his personal knowledge was not established, and what appears to be his
personal opinion that Claimant’s injury “could be due to a pre-existing condition.”
With the exception of explanation as to the rationale for not filing a
workers compensation claim, his statement is of no evidentiary value.
10. Mr. DeThomas testified that he believed Claimant had violated a safety rule by
climbing a ladder without a safety observer in violation of employer’s safety
policies, and that Claimant refused to return to work after his injury. However, no
credible evidence was admitted demonstrating that Claimant’s injury was caused
by or related to any alleged safety rule violation.
11. Claimant did not return to work for Employer following his injury. Claimant
submitted records indicating he returned to work from July 7, 2025 through the
present for Valiant Products Corporation. Claimant’s pay stub for the November
15 – 28, 2025 pay period shows Claimant’s year-to-date earnings of $20,766.98
3

at a regular rate of $26.00 per hour (i.e., 798.73 hours), the equivalent of
approximately twenty 40-hour work weeks. Claimant offered no credible evidence
demonstrating that he suffered a loss of earning capacity after July 7, 2025.
Conclusions of Law
Generally
A. The purpose of the Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado, §§ 8-40-101, et
seq., C.R.S., is to assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical
benefits to injured workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the
necessity of litigation. See § 8-40-102(1), C.R.S. Claimant shoulders the burden
of proving entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. See § 8-
43-201, C.R.S. A preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-
fact, after considering all of the evidence, to find that a fact is more probably true
than not. Page v. Clark, 592 P.2d 792 (Colo. 1979). The facts in a workers’
compensation case must be interpreted neutrally; neither in favor of the rights of
the claimant, nor in favor of the rights of respondents; and a workers’
compensation claim shall be decided on the merits. § 8-43-201, C.R.S.
B. Assessing weight, credibility, and sufficiency of evidence in Workers'
Compensation proceedings is the exclusive domain of the administrative law
judge. University Park Care Center v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 43 P.3d 637
(Colo. App. 2001). Even if other evidence in the record may have supported a
contrary inference, it is for the ALJ to resolve conflicts in the evidence, make
credibility determinations, and draw plausible inferences from the evidence. Id. at
641. When determining credibility, the fact finder should consider, among other
things, the consistency or inconsistency of the witness's testimony and actions;
the reasonableness or unreasonableness (probability or improbability) of the
testimony and actions; the motives of the witness; whether the testimony has
been contradicted; and bias, prejudice, or interest. Prudential Ins. Co. v. Cline, 57
P.2d 1205 (Colo. 1936); Bodensieck v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 183 P.3d
684 (Colo. App. 2008). The weight and credibility to be assigned expert
testimony is a matter within the discretion of the ALJ. Cordova v. Indus. Claim
4

Appeals Office, 55 P.3d 186 (Colo. App. 2002). To the extent expert testimony is
subject to conflicting interpretations, the ALJ may resolve the conflict by crediting
part or none of the testimony. Colorado Springs Motors Ltd. v. Indus. Comm’n,
441 P.2d 21 (Colo. 1968).
C. The ALJ's factual findings concern only evidence and inferences found to be
dispositive of the issues involved; the ALJ has not addressed every piece of
evidence or every inference that might lead to conflicting conclusions and has
rejected evidence contrary to the above findings as unpersuasive. Magnetic
Eng’g, Inc. v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 5 P.3d 385 (Colo. App. 2000).
Compensability
D. To establish a compensable injury an employee must prove by a preponderance
of the evidence that his injury arose out of the course and scope of employment
with his employer. § 8-41-301(1)(b), C.R.S. (2006); see City of Boulder v. Streeb,
706 P.2d 786, 791 (Colo. 1985). An injury occurs "in the course of” employment
when a claimant demonstrates that the injury occurred within the time and place
limits of his employment and during an activity that had some connection with his
work-related functions. Triad Painting Co. v. Blair, 812 P.2d 638, 641 (Colo.
1991). The "arising out of" requirement is narrower and requires the claimant to
demonstrate that the injury has its “origin in an employee's work-related functions
and is sufficiently related thereto to be considered part of the employee’s service
to the employer.” Popovich v. Irlando, 811 P.2d 379, 383 (Colo. 1991). A
compensable injury is one that causes disability or the need for medical
treatment. City of Boulder v. Payne, 426 P.2d 194 (1967); Mailand v. PSC Indus.
Outsourcing LP, W.C. No. 4-898-391-01, (ICAO Aug. 25, 2014).
E. Claimant has established by a preponderance of the evidence that he sustained
a work-related injury on April 11, 2025. Claimant credibly testified that he heard a
“pop” while removing window trim for Employer on April 11, 2025, and
experienced pain in his right shoulder. Claimant’s contemporaneous medical
records from UCHealth are consistent with the report, and demonstrate that
Claimant likely sustained, at a minimum, a shoulder sprain which required
5

treatment. Employer’s belief that Claimant sustained a “minor” sprain does not
render the injury non-compensable, nor excuse Employer from compliance with
the Workers’ Compensation Act.
F. Employer’s (or its insurance agent’s) apparent belief that Claimant’s shoulder
injury was the result of a pre-existing condition does not change the result. A pre-
existing disease or susceptibility to injury does not disqualify a claim if the
employment aggravates, accelerates, or combines with the pre-existing disease
to produce a disability or need for medical treatment. Duncan v. Indus. Claim
Appeals Office, 107 P.3d 999 (Colo. App. 2004); H & H Warehouse v. Vicory,
805 P.2d 1167 (Colo. App. 1990); Enriquez v. Americold, WC 4-960-513-01,
(ICAO, Oct. 2, 2015). “A compensable aggravation can be a worsened
preexisting condition, a trigger of symptoms from a dormant condition, an
acceleration of the natural course of the preexisting condition, or a combination
with the condition to produce disability.” Bryant v. Mesa Cty. Valley Sch. Dist. 51,
W.C. No. 5-102-109-001 (ICAO, Mar. 18, 2020).
G. “To prove an aggravation, a claimant need not show an injury objectively caused
any identifiable structural change to their underlying anatomy. Rather, a purely
symptomatic aggravation is a sufficient basis for an award of medical benefits if it
caused the claimant to need treatment he would not otherwise have required but
for the accident.” In re Claim of Frank O’Neil Cambria, W.C. No. 5-066-531-002
(ICAO May 7, 2019). Compensability of aggravation cases turns on whether work
activities made the preexisting condition worse in some manner or simply
demonstrated the natural progression of the preexisting condition. Bryant, supra.
H. Although the record contains no evidence that Claimant had a pre-existing
shoulder condition, even if Claimant’s injury was an aggravation of a pre-existing
condition, it constitutes a compensable injury under the Colorado Workers’
Compensation Act.
Medical Treatment
I. Under section 8-42-101(1)(a), C.R.S., employers are liable for authorized
medical treatment that is reasonable and necessary to cure or relieve the effects
6

of the industrial injury. See Owens v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 49 P.3d 1187,
1188 (Colo. App. 2002). Because Claimant has established that he sustained a
compensable injury, he is entitled to all reasonable, and necessary medical
treatment rendered to cure or relieve the effects of his industrial injury.
J. Employer is therefore liable for all of Claimant’s reasonable and necessary
medical expenses related to the April 11, 2025 injury, pursuant to the Colorado
Medical Fee Schedule.
Authorized Treating Physician
K. Section 8-43-404(5)(a), C.R.S., permits an employer or insurer to select the
treating physician in the first instance. Yeck v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 996
P.2d 228 (Colo. App. 1999). However, the Colorado Workers’ Compensation Act
requires that respondents must provide injured workers with a list of at least four
designated treatment providers. §8-43-404(5)(a)(I)(A), C.R.S. Rule 8-2 (A)(2)
clarifies that, “[a] copy of the written designated provider list must be given to the
injured worker in a verifiable manner within seven (7) business days following the
date the employer has notice of the injury.” The term “business days” refers to
any day other than a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday. W.C.R.P. 1-2 (C).
L. An employer is deemed notified of an injury when it has “some knowledge of the
accompanying facts connecting the injury or illness with the employment and
indicating to a reasonably conscientious manager that the case might involve a
potential compensation claim.” Bunch v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 148 P.3d
381, 383 (Colo. App. 2006). If upon notice of the injury the employer does not
timely designate an ATP, the right of selection passes to the claimant. Rogers v.
Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 746 P.2d 565 (Colo. App. 1987), see also W.C.R.P.
8-2 (E) (“If the employer fails to supply the required designated provider list in
accordance with this rule, the injured worker may select an authorized treating
physician or chiropractor of their choosing.”) Where a claimant has signified “by
words or conduct that he has chosen a physician to treat the industrial injury,” he
has made physician “selection.” In re Claim of Murphy-Tafoya, W.C. No. 5-153-
600-001 (ICAO, Sept. 1, 2021).
7

M. The evidence establishes that Claimant informed Employer, through Mr.
DeThomas of his injury on April 11, 2025. Accordingly, Employer was obligated
to provide Claimant with a list of designated providers within seven business
days. Employer has neither presented evidence nor claimed that a list of medical
providers was delivered to Claimant. That Employer did not believe Claimant’s
injury was significant, or that Employer’s insurance agent believed Claimant had
aggravated a pre-existing condition does not relieve Employer of the obligation to
provide a designated provider list.
N. Claimant has established that Employer did not provide him a list of designated
providers as required by the Act. As such, the right of selection of designated
providers passed to Claimant.
O. The care Claimant received on April 11, 2025 constitutes emergency treatment
immediately following his injury for which Employer is liable. § 8-42-101(1)(a),
C.R.S.; Sims v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 797 P.2d 777 (Colo. App. 1990). The
evidence is unclear whether the treatment Claimant sought at County Line
Chiropractic was for his work-related injury or for other conditions. As such, the
ALJ finds that Claimant may select an authorized treating physician for
evaluation and treatment of his work-related shoulder injury.
Temporary Disability Benefits/Termination
P. To prove entitlement to temporary total disability (TTD), a claimant must prove
that the industrial injury caused a disability lasting more than three work shifts, he
left work because of the disability, and the disability resulted in an actual wage
loss. See §§ 8-42-103(1)(a) & (b) C.R.S.; Anderson v. Longmont Toyota, 102
P.3d 323 (Colo. 2004); City of Colorado Springs v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off.,
954 P.2d 637 (Colo. App. 1997). Section 8-42-103(1)(a) requires a claimant to
establish a causal connection between a work-related injury and a subsequent
wage loss to obtain temporary disability benefits. The term “disability” connotes
two elements: (1) medical incapacity evidenced by loss or restriction of bodily
function; and (2) impairment of wage-earning capacity as demonstrated by
claimant's inability to resume his or her prior work. Culver v. Ace Electric, 971
P.2d 641, 649 (Colo. 1999). The impairment of earning capacity element of
8

disability may be evidenced by a complete inability to work or by restrictions
which impair the claimant's ability effectively and properly to perform his or her
regular employment. Ortiz v. Charles J. Murphy & Co., 964 P.2d 595, 597 (Colo.
App. 1998). Because there is no requirement that a claimant must produce
evidence of medical restrictions, a claimant’s testimony alone is sufficient to
demonstrate a disability. Lymburn v. Symbios Logic, 952 P.2d 831, 833 (Colo.
App. 1997).
Q. The Workers' Compensation Act prohibits a claimant from receiving temporary
disability benefits if the claimant is responsible for termination of the employment
relationship. Gilmore v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 187 P.3d 1129, (Colo. App.
2008); The termination statutes -- §§ 8-42-103(1)(g), 8-42-105(4)(a), C.R.S. --
provide: “In cases where it is determined that a temporarily disabled employee is
responsible for termination of employment, the resulting wage loss shall not be
attributable to the on-the-job injury.” See also In re of Davis, W.C. No. 4-631-681
(ICAO Apr. 24, 2006).
R. “Under the termination statutes, sections 8-42-103(1)(g) and 8-42-105(4), an
employer bears the burden of establishing by a preponderance of the evidence
that a claimant was terminated for cause or was responsible for the separation
from employment.” Gilmore, 187 P.3d at 1132. “Generally, the question of
whether the claimant acted volitionally, and therefore is ‘responsible’ for a
termination from employment, is a question of fact to be decided by the ALJ,
based on consideration of the totality of the circumstances.” Gonzales v. Indus.
Comm’n, 740 P.2d 999 (Colo. 1987); Windom v. Lawrence Constr. Co., W.C. No.
4-487-966 (ICAO Nov. 1, 2002). In re Olaes, WC. No. 4-782-977 (ICAO April 12,
2011). Implicit in the termination statutes is a requirement that Respondents
prove Claimant committed an “act” which formed the basis for her termination.
Ultimately, the question of whether the claimant was responsible for the
termination is one of fact for determination by the ALJ. Apex Trans., Inc. v. Indus.
Claim Appeals Office, 321 P.3d 630, 632 (Colo. App. 2014).
S. Claimant has failed to establish an entitlement to temporary disability benefits,
and Employer has established that Claimant was responsible for his own
9

termination. After his initial evaluation at the UCHealth ER, Claimant was
released to return to work on April 15, 2025. Although Claimant was not subject
to work restrictions, Employer offered Claimant modified duty in writing, by asking
Claimant to come to the office to work on phone duty. Claimant elected not to
accept the modified employment and did not return to work for Employer
thereafter. Claimant then began new, full time employment with Valiant Products
Corporation on July 7, 2025. Claimant’s refusal to return to work for Employer
constitutes a voluntary resignation for which he was responsible. Claimant’s
wage loss is a result of his resignation, rather than his injury, and he is not
entitled to temporary disability benefits.
Penalties for Uninsured Employer
T. Section 8-43-408(1), C.R.S., provides that where an employer has not complied
with the Act’s insurance provisions, an injured worker may claim compensation
and benefits under the Act. Pursuant to section 8-43-408(2), C.R.S.: “In all cases
where compensation is awarded under the terms of this section, the director or
an administrative law judge of the division shall compute and require the
employer to pay to a trustee designated by the director or administrative law
judge an amount equal to the present value of all unpaid compensation or
benefits computed at the rate of four percent per annum; or, in lieu thereof, such
employer, within ten days after the date of such order, shall file a bond with the
director or administrative law judge signed by two or more responsible sureties to
be approved by the director or by some surety company authorized to do
business within the state of Colorado. The bond shall be in such form and
amount as prescribed and fixed by the director and shall guarantee the payment
of the compensation or benefits as awarded. The filing of any appeal, including a
petition for review, shall not relieve the employer of the obligation under this
subsection (2) to pay the designated sum to a trustee or to file a bond with the
director or administrative law judge.” The term “compensation” refers to disability
benefits. In Re of Shier, W.C. No. 4-573-910 (ICAO Dec. 15, 2005). Where an
employer is uninsured at the time of an injury; the provisions of section 8-43-
408(2) are mandatory.
10

U. Once a claimant establishes a compensable injury, the burden shifts to the
employer to establish a limitation of its liability by proof it had workers'
compensation insurance. McManus v. Oil Tools Limited, W.C. No. 4-481-926
(April 29, 2002). No credible evidence was admitted at hearing demonstrating
that Employer had in place workers’ compensation insurance at the time of
Claimant’s injury. Although Mr. Cheese’s statement and Mr. DeThomas’s text
messages imply that Employer was insured, Employer has not provided proof of
insurance and did not submit Claimant’s claim to an insurer. Section 8-43-103(1),
C.R.S., which requires employers to give notice to the Division and their
insurance carrier within ten days after an employee injury. Similarly, WCRP 5-
2(A), provides that an employer must report any work-related injury to the
employer’s insurer within ten days of notice or knowledge of the injury. The Rule
also provides that “An employer who does not provide the required notice may be
subject to penalties or other sanctions.”
V. Based on the evidence presented at hearing, the ALJ concludes that Employer
was uninsured at the time of Claimant’s injury and is obligated to either pay the
trustee or post a bond in the amount of the compensation and benefits to which
Claimant would be entitled.
W. Section 8-42-101 (3)(a)(I), C.R.S., provides that the fees charged by medical
providers for workers’ compensation injuries may not exceed those set forth in
the medical fee schedule adopted by the Director. No credible evidence was
admitted demonstrating that the fees charged by Claimant’s medical providers
comply with the fee schedule. Because the evidence was insufficient to
determine the amount of Claimant’s medical bills due under the Medical Fee
Schedule, the evidence is insufficient to determine the amount Employer is
required to pay to the trustee. This issue is reserved for future determination.
Additional Liability Under § 8-43-408(5), C.R.S.
A. Section 8-43-408(5), C.R.S., provides: In addition to any compensation paid or
ordered in accordance with this section or articles 40 to 47 of this title 8, an
employer who is not in compliance with the insurance provisions of those articles
at the time an employee suffers a compensable injury or occupational disease
11

shall pay an amount equal to twenty-five percent of the compensation or benefits
to which the employee is entitled to the Colorado uninsured employer fund
created in section 8-67-105.
B. Because the amount of compensation or benefits to which Claimant is entitled
cannot be determined based on the evidence presented, the ALJ cannot
determine Employer’s additional liability under § 8-43-408 (5), C.R.S. The issue
is reserved for future determination.
Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. Claimant sustained a compensable injury arising out of the course of his
employment with Employer on April 11, 2025.
2. Claimant is entitled to reasonable and necessary medical benefits to cure or
relieve the effects of his April 11, 2025 workplace injury. The treatment Claimant
received at UCHealth on April 11, 2025 was reasonable and necessary. Claimant
has failed to establish that the treatment he received from County Line
Chiropractic was reasonable, necessary, or related to his workplace injury.
3. Claimant is entitled to select his authorized treating physician for his workplace
injury.
4. Claimant’s request for temporary disability benefits is denied. Determination of
Claimant’s average weekly wage is moot.
5. Employer is liable for payment of Claimant’s medical expenses pursuant
to the Division of Workers’ Compensation Medical Fee Schedule. The
monetary amount of medical benefits is reserved for future determination,
and no payment is due until the benefits to which Claimant is entitled is
established. Because Employer is liable for payment of Claimant’s medical
costs associated with his work injury, no medical provider shall seek to
recover such costs from Claimant, pursuant to § 8-42-101(4), C.R.S.
a. In lieu of payment of the above compensation and benefits to the
Claimant, Employer shall:
12

b. Upon determination of the appropriate sum, deposit said sum with
the Division of Workers’ Compensation as trustee, to secure the
payment of all unpaid TTD benefits awarded. The check shall be
payable to and sent to the Division of Workers; Compensation
Division Trustee, c/o Mariya Cassin, 633 17th Street, Suite 400,
Denver, CO 80202; or
c. File a bond the Division of Workers’ Compensation within ten (10)
days of the date of any order determining amount of the
compensation and benefits to which Claimant is entitled:
i. Signed by two or more responsible sureties who have
received prior approval of the Division of Workers’
Compensation; or
ii. Issued by a surety company authorized to do business in
Colorado.
d. The bond shall guarantee payment of the compensation and benefit
awarded.
6. Employer is responsible for additional liability under § 8-43-408(5), C.R.S.,
for failure to maintain workers’ compensation insurance. Employer shall
pay the Colorado uninsured employer fund an amount equal to 25% of
compensation and benefits to which Claimant is entitled. The amount of
such additional liability is reserved for future determination, and no such
payment is due until the amount of additional liability has been
established.
7. All matters not determined herein are reserved for future determination.
NOTE: If you are dissatisfied with the ALJ's order, you may file a Petition to Review the
order with the Denver Office of Administrative Courts, 1525 Sherman St., 4th Floor,
Denver, CO 80203. You must file your Petition to Review within twenty (20) days after
mailing or service of the order, as indicated on the certificate of mailing or service;
otherwise, the ALJ's order will be final. You may file the Petition to Review by mail, as
long as the certificate of mailing attached to your petition shows: (1) That you mailed it
within twenty (20) days after mailing or service of the order of the ALJ; and (2) That you
13

mailed it to the above address for the Denver Office of Administrative Courts. You may
file your Petition to Review electronically by emailing the Petition to Review to the
following email address: oac-ptr@state.co.us. If the Petition to Review is emailed to the
aforementioned email address, the Petition to Review is deemed filed in Denver
pursuant to OACRP 27 and Section 8-43-301, C.R.S. If the Petition to Review is filed by
email to the proper email address, it does not need to be mailed to the Denver Office of
Administrative Courts. For further information regarding procedures to follow when filing
a Petition to Review, see Rule 27, OACRP. You may access a petition to review form
at: http://www.colorado.gov/dpa/oac/forms-WC.htm.

14
